L219: ## SUMMARY
L220: STAT3 is an oncogenic transcription factor that activates cancer cell signaling and induces an immunosuppressive immune environment, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Transcription factors are exceptionally challenging targets and there are no Food and Drug Administration-approved STAT3 inhibitors.
L221: We previously reported positive pharmacodynamics of a linear STAT3 decoy oligonucleotide administered intratumorally in a Phase 0 trial in patients with head and neck cancer squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Here, we describe the anti-tumor and immune effects of a systemically administered cyclic STAT3 decoy (CS3D) in immunocompetent HNSCC murine models and the safety and efficacy of CS3D in a clinical trial in pet cats with HNSCC.
L222: Responders in the clinical trial (35% disease control rate) showed significant differences in selected peripheral blood immune parameters as well as elevated PD-1 expression in the tumors compared with non-responders. These findings support a clinical trial of CS3D in HNSCC patients.
L223: Keywords: STAT3, cyclic STAT3 decoy, head and neck cancer, oral cancer, STAT3 inhibitor, clinical trial, feline oral cancer
L224: ## eTOC Blurb:
L225: 
L226: Grandis et al. evaluate the activity of a cyclic oligonucleotide inhibitor of STAT3, CS3D, in immunocompetent models of mouse head and neck cancer and in a clinical trial of pet cats with oral cancer. CS3D has low toxicity and modulation of immune parameters is associated with anti-tumor activity.

L228: 【35†Image: graphic file with name nihms-2102076-f0008.jpg†cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov】
L229: ## INTRODUCTION
L230: 
L231: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is an oncogenic transcription factor that is hyperactivated in most solid tumors and hematopoietic malignancies. Its role in stimulating tumor cell proliferation/survival, inducing immunosuppression, and promoting cancer drug resistance makes STAT3 a particularly attractive therapeutic target for most cancers.^{【36†1】–【37†5】}
L232: Like all transcription factors, STAT3 has long been considered an exceptionally challenging target due to its intracellular localization and lack of enzymatic activity.
L233: To address the gap in clinical STAT3 inhibitors, we designed a 15-bp duplex oligonucleotide with free ends, termed the STAT3 decoy, which resembles a STAT3 response element, binds selectively to activated STAT3, competitively inhibits STAT3 binding to target gene promoters, induces head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) apoptosis, and suppresses xenograft tumor growth.^{【38†4】,【39†6】–【40†10】} A Phase 0 clinical trial^{【41†11】} involving intratumoral injection of the STAT3 decoy in human HNSCC patients undergoing surgical resection with curative intent demonstrated downmodulation of STAT3 target genes in resected tumors after a single injection.^{【42†12】} A cyclic version of the STAT3 decoy exhibits improved thermal stability and nuclease resistance, and inhibited the growth of xenograft tumors following systemic delivery in immunodeficient mice.^{【42†12】–【43†15】}
L234: The impact of cyclic STAT3 decoy (CS3D) administration on the immune system has not been studied, limiting the design of further clinical trials with this promising anti-cancer agent.
L235: An antisense oligonucleotide targeting STAT3 mRNA (AZD9150, danvatirsen) has shown safety and activity in early phase studies in lymphoma and lung cancer where it reversed a suppressive tumor microenvironment and promoted proinflammatory gene expression changes in patient tumors.^{【44†16】,【45†17】} Cumulative evidence underscores the importance of the immune system in HNSCC progression.^{【46†18】–【47†22】}
L236: In the present study, we tested the CS3D in multiple different preclinical HNSCC models (murine and feline cell lines, organoids containing immune components, and immunocompetent xenograft tumors) and found evidence of dose-dependent anti-tumor activity. Depletion of CD8^{+} T-cells reversed the anti-tumor effects in vivo, strongly implicating the impact of the STAT3 decoy on the tumor microenvironment.
L237: While testing novel anti-cancer agents in both immunodeficient and immunocompetent mouse models of cancer can demonstrate anti-tumor mechanisms, these models do not reflect the heterogeneity of spontaneously arising malignancies. Naturally occurring tumors in pet animals provide an opportunity to test novel cancer therapeutics and validate preclinical findings.
L238: Oral squamous cell carcinoma is commonly diagnosed in pet cats, is locally aggressive, and considered incurable.^{【48†23】,【49†24】} Feline oral cancer is generally fatal within 2 to 3 months and radiation treatment provides only a modest survival benefit.^{【50†25】–【51†27】} There is remarkable clinical, histopathologic, and immunologic similarity between feline and human HNSCC.^{【48†23】,【49†24】,【52†28】–【53†30】} Both species have similar environmental exposures, genetic and biologic diversity, and mature immune systems.
L239: Human and feline HNSCCs are both naturally occurring and heterogeneous and feline tumors exhibit similar expression and mutational profiles of key biomarkers, including EGFR, VEGF, p16, p53, and Rb.^{【48†23】,【49†24】,【52†28】,【54†29】,【55†31】–【56†35】} Hyperactivation of STAT3, as assessed by phosphorylation, has also been reported in 48% of feline HNSCC tumors.^{【57†36】}
L240: Because of the similarities between human and feline HNSCC, we sought to study the biologic effects of the CS3D in pet cats who develop HNSCC to inform the design of future human trials and identify biomarkers. A total of twenty cats were enrolled and treated on a Phase I protocol. There was no evidence of a dose-limiting toxicity even at the highest dose tested (10 mg/kg).
L241: Using RECIST criteria^{【58†37】}, two cats experienced partial tumor responses and five cats demonstrated stable disease while the remaining thirteen cats showed tumor progression for an overall disease control rate of 35%. Correlative biomarker studies including RNAseq analysis of the tumor biopsies and flow cytometry of the peripheral blood demonstrated distinct differences between responding and non-responding cats in their tumor gene expression profiles as well as circulating immune cell populations.
L242: These cumulative findings suggest that treatment with this first-in-class STAT3 inhibitor is safe and may be an effective anti-cancer strategy, exerting its effects on both tumor and immune cells. Further clinical testing in both companion animals and human patients with cancer is warranted.
L243: ## RESULTS
L244: ### Cyclic STAT3 decoy (CS3D) reduces cell viability and the levels of STAT3 target genes in murine HNSCC cell lines
L245: We previously reported that intravenous administration of CS3D inhibits the growth of human HNSCC cell line-derived xenograft tumors in immunodeficient mice.^{【42†12】,【59†13】} Because genetic inactivation of the STAT3 gene in immune cells promotes anti-tumor immunity,^{【60†38】–【61†44】} we sought to determine the impact of the CS3D in well-characterized immunocompetent murine models of HNSCC prior to conducting clinical evaluation of CS3D in pet cats.
L246: MOC1, MOC22, and mEER are murine HNSCC cell lines that grow well as tumors in immunocompetent, syngeneic C57BL/6 mice and represent both human papilloma virus (HPV)-negative (MOC1, MOC22) and HPV-positive (mEER) HNSCC.^{【62†45】–【63†49】} We first examined the impact of CS3D on the viability of MOC1, MOC22, and mEER in vitro (【64†Figure 1A】). As controls, cells were left untreated or were treated with Lipofectamine alone, or with Lipofectamine plus a scrambled sequence version of the cyclic decoy (SCR).
L247: Treatment of each cell line with 1 μM CS3D resulted in a roughly 40-60% loss of cell viability after 48 hours. By contrast, treatment with 1 μM SCR resulted in less than a 10% loss of cell viability. To confirm the inhibitory impact of CS3D on the expression of STAT3 target genes in the murine HNSCC cell lines, we analyzed the expression of three representative target genes (VEGF, CCND1, Bcl-X_{L}) 24 hours after treatment with CS3D or SCR (1 μM).
L248: In all three cell lines, treatment with CS3D resulted in a statistically significant reduction in VEGF, CCND1, and Bcl-X_{L} mRNA levels when compared with SCR treatment (【64†Figure 1B】). An exception to this was CCND1 mRNA in MOC1 where expression only trended downward with CS3D treatment (p = 0.079). Collectively, these results show that CS3D reduced cell viability and the expression of STAT3 target genes and in both HPV-negative and HPV-positive murine HNSCC cell line models.

L258: ### CS3D inhibits growth and ATP production in murine HNSCC tumor organoids
L259: We next sought to determine the impact of CS3D treatment on murine HNSCC models grown ex vivo and retaining 3-dimensional (3D) tumor architecture and associated tumor-infiltrating immune cells.
L260: For this purpose, MOC1, MOC22, and mEER cells were grown as subcutaneous tumors in immunocompetent C57BL/6 mice and excised tumor tissues containing both tumor epithelial cells and immune cells were embedded in collagen gels and used to generate organoids using the air-liquid interface (ALI) method.^{【68†50】} A fourth murine HNSCC model, 4MOSC1, derived from C57BL/6 mice,^{【69†51】} was also incorporated in these studies.
L261: After 7 days of culture, we successfully generated organoids from all 4 murine HNSCC tumor models. Comparison of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained organoid sections with H&E-stained sections of the corresponding primary tumors demonstrated that the organoids retained architectural similarity with the original primary tumors (【70†Figure 2A】–【70†D】).
L262: The organoids exhibited a keratinizing, well-to-moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma morphology and a mild inflammatory infiltrate (【70†Figure 2A】–【70†D】, 【71†Supplementary Figure S1】). Immunofluorescence staining demonstrated the expression of E-cadherin-positive tumor-associated epithelial cells, vimentin-positive fibroblasts, and CD45-positive immune cells in both the organoids and the primary tumors from which the organoids were derived (【71†Supplementary Figure S1】).

Statistical comparisons used one-way ANOVA and were adjusted for the multiplicity of the comparisons across all 4 models using Sidak’s method.
L271: We next examined the impact of CS3D (1 μM) treatment on organoid viability and ATP production (【70†Figure 2E】–【70†L】). As controls, organoids were treated with SCR (1 μM), Lipofectamine alone, or left untreated. In addition, the commonly used HNSCC chemotherapy agent cisplatin served as a positive control.
L272: Seven days after treatment organoids were processed into single cell suspensions and stained with trypan blue for determination of percent cell viability or were incubated with CellTiter-Glo 3D cell viability reagent to determine ATP levels. When compared to treatment with SCR, treatment with CS3D resulted in significant reduction of cell viability and ATP levels in all four organoid models.
L273: Hence, CS3D inhibited the growth of the murine HNSCC models in both 2D cultures and 3D cultures containing immune components derived from the primary tumors.
L274: ### CS3D inhibits the growth of murine HNSCC tumors in immunocompetent mice
L275: CS3D has been shown to inhibit the growth of human tumor xenografts in immunodeficient mice.^{【42†12】,【59†13】,【43†15】} Here, we tested the impact of CS3D treatment on the growth of murine HNSCC tumors in immunocompetent mice in 3 different models (【74†Figure 3】). MOC22, mEER, and 4MOSC1 were grown as subcutaneous tumors in the flanks of syngeneic, wild-type C57BL/6 mice.
L276: We elected to implant the cells subcutaneously since studies assessing the growth of murine orthotopic (buccal or floor-of-mouth) HNSCC tumors are limited by the morbidity of oral tumors on the ability of the mouse to eat, thereby creating a very narrow window to study therapeutic effects.
L277: In addition, others have observed similar kinetics of immune infiltration in subcutaneously and orthotopically implanted immunocompetent oral cancer cells.^{【75†52】} Tumor-bearing mice were randomized for treatment with vehicle (saline), SCR (10 mg/kg), or CS3D (5 or 10 mg/kg), 5 times/week via tail vein intravenous delivery. The concentrations of CS3D chosen for use were based on pilot dose-response data in human HNSCC xenografts.
L278: Treatment of the MOC22 model with CS3D resulted in potent, dose-dependent inhibition of tumor growth, with complete inhibition seen with the 10 mg/kg dose (【74†Figure 3A】). Inhibition of MOC22 tumor growth was associated with induction of apoptosis, as demonstrated by immunoblotting of tumor lysates for cleavage of PARP protein (【71†Supplementary Figure S2A】).
L279: Similar dose-dependent inhibition of tumor growth was observed with the mEER model, although the 10 mg/kg CS3D dose was somewhat less effective than in MOC22 tumors (【74†Figure 3B】). In the 4MOSC1 model, only the 5 mg/kg dose of CS3D was tested, where partial inhibition of tumor growth was seen (【74†Figure 3C】). By contrast, in all three murine HNSCC models treatment with the scrambled cyclic decoy, SCR, had no impact on tumor growth.

L295: Our results demonstrated that CS3D treatment inhibited the growth of HNSCC tumors in immunocompetent mice and raised the question whether immune cells contributed to these anti-tumor effects. CD8-positive (CD8^{+}) T-cells are major effectors of anti-tumor immunity and activation of STAT3 in tumor infiltrating CD8^{+} inhibits the activity of these cells.
L296: Therefore, we investigated the role of CD8^{+} cells in the anti-tumor activity of CS3D by performing an immunodepletion experiment (【74†Figure 3D】 & 【74†3E】). C57BL/6 mice harboring MOC22 tumors were first given intraperitoneal injections of anti-CD8 or anti-IgG control (0.5 mg/mouse/dose) on 3 consecutive days. Twenty-four hours after the third dose, two mice from each group were sacrificed and their spleens and tumors were harvested for flow cytometric analysis of CD8^{+} cells.
